prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part prize on B006 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific case is unchanged by the exchange: proglucagon processing, the active truncated GLP-1(7-36) peptide, its glucose-dependent insulinotropic action in humans and the wider biology of satiety and gastric emptying form a complete discovery arc. Large independent randomized trials in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease have confirmed the clinical consequence, and nobody in round 1 argued that the work is premature. The citation is worded around physiology and the identification of the active form, so it makes no claim to be the first to find the peptide, which is the point on which the record is contested. I have not changed my preferred configuration. The chair's question on a second part did not move me: B006 already uses all three names, and adding a second part would mean dropping one of them without a scientific reason.
statement.case_against: The weak point is still attribution, and the round-1 exchange sharpened it without resolving it. Habener is outside the supplied names, Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested, and the citation leaves out the acylation and half-life-extension work that produced liraglutide and semaglutide. A critic could say the prize honours the academic steps and passes over the step that put the drug in patients. That criticism is fair, and a reader could take my configuration as partly arbitrary on the third name. I am also still relying on recalled history, not on documents, for who showed what and when.

responses.point: Moved off Mojsov because naming her without Habener makes the peptide-identification chapter hard to defend, and proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen with a citation naming both physiology and long-acting therapy.
responses.response: The Habener problem is real, and I take it more seriously than I did in round 1. My answer is that an incomplete credit on a contested early step does not justify replacing that step with an industrial one. The three-person cap leaves someone out under either trio. If we drop the identification of the active peptide, the citation no longer explains why GLP-1 can work as a therapy. I would keep Mojsov and word the citation around the identification of the active form, not a first-discovery claim. I do accept her point that the committee should state openly who is omitted and why.

responses.point: Stresses that the committee should state its translation principle openly because it also bears on B004 and B040, and prefers Knudsen as the third name.
responses.response: I agree the principle must be stated, and I think it favours my trio. If the prize credits an industrial optimisation step here, we should do the same for B040 and B004, where the design of the drug or the construct carries comparable weight. I would rather hold to a rule that the prize rewards the discovery of the biological principle and the entity that carries it. That rule credits Mojsov's identification of the active peptide and not Knudsen's analogue engineering. In round 1 I said I could accept the swap if the citation named the therapeutic achievement. After this round I am less willing, because the swap would change the principle, not only a name.

responses.point: Moved to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and the chair asks whether any second part should be considered and which B006 name would be dropped.
responses.response: I welcome the chair's move and agree that the third name is the only open question on B006. On his question about a second part, I would not add one. Dropping any of the three would give up a core contributor to the GLP-1 case for a candidate that, by our own discussion, has an attribution or maturity limit. I would also support the chair's request for documentary evidence on the Mojsov and Habener priority question. Without that evidence, I want the citation to say only what the physiology and the identification of the active form show.

responses.point: Ranks B039 second as a clean, fundamental cell-biology discovery with Walter and Mori as the two decisive contributors, and notes that long-term safety data on GLP-1 therapies are still accumulating.
responses.response: Her attribution argument for B039 is the best on the shortlist, and I keep it as my second alternative. I still disagree that it should compete with B006 this year. The UPR therapeutic payoff is early, and Ron, Kaufman and Kozutsumi keep the credit from being as clean as the two names imply. On her safety point, the ongoing long-term safety data for GLP-1 agonists do not undercut the discovery. They concern the later clinical chapter, and the physiological discovery stands independently of them.

uncertainties: Whether the documentary record supports crediting Mojsov for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide alongside or ahead of Habener, and whether omitting Habener is acceptable.
Whether the committee will treat analogue engineering (Knudsen) as discovery or as optimisation, and whether it would apply the same rule to B004 and B040.
Whether Eshhar's omission and Rosenberg's place make B004 defensible if the committee wanted a second part.
My accounts of priority and credit come from recalled history, not from primary documents.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I have documented co-authorship with fellow member Sten Linnarsson and with Jonas Frisen, but neither is connected to B006 or to any other shortlisted candidate, and shared Karolinska affiliation is not a conflict. No update since round 1.
